classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that aces are a subset of serves landing in, subtract their probability to obtain a non-ace successful serve, and count the four possible positions of that serve.

content.prompt: A tennis player finds that, on average, he gets his serve in eight out of every ten attempts and that he serves an ace, a serve which is in the boundaries and not touched by his opponent, once every fifteen serves. He serves four times. Assuming that successive serves are independent events, find, correct to six decimal places, the probability that:

children.label: b
children.prompt: he hits at least three aces,

answer.worked:
Let $X$ be the number of aces. Then $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}\left(4,\frac1{15}\right)$.
$$\begin{align*}P(X\ge3)&=P(X=3)+P(X=4)\\&=\binom43\left(\frac1{15}\right)^3\left(\frac{14}{15}\right)+\left(\frac1{15}\right)^4\\&\approx0.001126.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: he hits exactly three aces and the other serve lands in.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{in but not an ace})&=\frac45-\frac1{15}\\&=\frac{11}{15}.\end{align*}$$
There are $\binom43$ choices for the three ace positions.
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{three aces and the other serve in})&=\binom43\left(\frac1{15}\right)^3\left(\frac{11}{15}\right)\\&\approx0.000869.\end{align*}$$
